questions.stem:
A county has hired a construction manager as constructor for a 120,000 sf justice center. The CM will set a guaranteed maximum price at the end of design development. The county also wants site work and foundations to start three months before the rest of the construction documents are finished.

Which documentation should the architect plan for? Check the three that apply.

options.text: A GMP set of DD drawings and outline specifications
options.explanation: Correct. The CM prices the GMP from the DD-level set.

options.text: Review of the CM's assumptions and clarifications list
options.explanation: Correct. The assumptions define what the GMP includes and must be reconciled with the documents.

options.text: An early-release site and foundation package
options.explanation: Correct. The early start needs its own package, completed and permitted first.

options.text: A complete hard-bid set before the CM is engaged
options.explanation: CMc engages the CM during design. A full hard-bid set isn't the basis.

options.text: Instructions to bidders for general contractors
options.explanation: The CM is already selected, so no general contractors bid.

options.text: Record drawings issued with the GMP
options.explanation: Record drawings come after construction.

questions.explanation: CMc: GMP set, reconciled assumptions, early-release packages.

questions.stem:
A university plans to procure a new laboratory building through design-build. It has hired an architect as its bridging consultant to prepare the documents the design-builders will propose against. The university wants to control the program and quality but also wants competitive, innovative proposals.

How far should the bridging documents be developed?

options.text: To full construction documents, so proposals are comparable
options.explanation: Fully detailed documents remove the design-builder's role and shift design responsibility to the owner.

options.text: Enough to define program, concept and performance
options.explanation: Correct. Bridging documents define what the owner requires and leave the detailed design to the design-builder.

options.text: Only a one-page program summary
options.explanation: Too little definition produces proposals that can't be compared and invites quality disputes.

options.text: To the same level as a DBB bid set, without specifications
options.explanation: A bid-set level of drawings has the same over-detailing problem.

questions.explanation: Bridging documents: program, concept and performance criteria, often about 30% design.

questions.stem:
For a design-build data center procured with bridging documents, the owner requires the cooling system to hold specific temperature and humidity ranges, with stated redundancy and a minimum efficiency. The owner doesn't want to dictate the equipment, and the design-builder's engineer will design the system.

Which type of specification should the bridging architect use for the cooling system?

options.text: Proprietary, naming the preferred manufacturer
options.explanation: Naming products limits the design-builder's choices.

options.text: Descriptive, defining components and installation
options.explanation: Describing components dictates the design the owner wants to leave open.

options.text: Performance, defining the required results
options.explanation: Correct. Performance specifications state the required results and leave the design to the design-builder.

options.text: Reference standard, citing an industry test method
options.explanation: Citing a standard alone doesn't define the owner's performance requirements.

questions.explanation: Design-build and delegated design use performance specifications.

questions.stem:
A school district is building a high school as a fast-track project, with three separately bid prime contracts: site and utilities, building shell, and interiors and MEP. On a past project like this, gaps between contracts led to several disputes over who furnished temporary power and who patched slabs after MEP rough-in.

Which documentation practices would best prevent these disputes? Check the three that apply.

options.text: A written scope description for each package
options.explanation: Correct. Narrative scopes define each contract's responsibilities.

options.text: Drawings that show the limits of each package
options.explanation: Correct. Graphic limits show where each contract starts and stops.

options.text: A responsibility list for shared and interface items
options.explanation: Correct. Shared items such as temporary power and patching need assigned owners.

options.text: One combined specification with no package divisions
options.explanation: A combined spec doesn't define what each prime contractor includes.

options.text: Leaving interface items to the contractors to resolve
options.explanation: Unassigned items become disputes and change orders.

options.text: Issuing all packages at the same time
options.explanation: Fast-tracking staggers the packages, and timing doesn't fix scope gaps.

questions.explanation: Multiple prime packages need defined scopes, graphic limits and assigned interface items.

questions.stem:
Construction documents for a performing arts center are complete and will be bid as a stipulated sum. The owner hasn't yet chosen its audiovisual and theatrical lighting equipment, and is still weighing two very different systems. It expects to decide within four months, well after the construction contract is awarded.

How should the bid documents handle the equipment?

options.text: Include an allowance for the equipment
options.explanation: Correct. An allowance carries a set amount in the bids for a decision that isn't final, and the contract sum is adjusted later.

options.text: Leave the equipment out and add it later by change order
options.explanation: Leaving known scope out makes bids incomplete and invites premium pricing later.

options.text: Specify one system now, to be confirmed later
options.explanation: Specifying a system the owner may not choose invites a costly change.

options.text: Ask each bidder to propose its own system
options.explanation: Bidder-chosen systems make the bids impossible to compare.

questions.explanation: Use allowances for owner decisions that aren't final in a DBB bid set.

questions.stem:
Bidding for a county office building produced six addenda that changed 40 drawing sheets and 12 specification sections. After award, the contractor asks for a single set of documents with all the addenda folded in, so its field staff and subcontractors work from one set. The owner agrees this would help.

Which deliverable is being requested?

options.text: Record drawings
options.explanation: Record drawings document construction as built, after the work.

options.text: Conformed documents
options.explanation: Correct. Conformed documents incorporate the addenda into the contract set. B101 lists them as a supplemental service.

options.text: Shop drawings
options.explanation: Shop drawings are prepared by the contractor for fabrication and installation.

options.text: As-designed record drawings
options.explanation: These document the design, not the bid addenda.

questions.explanation: Conformed set = bid documents + addenda, for construction.

questions.stem:
At the end of construction of a hospital wing, the owner asks the architect for a set of drawings showing the final locations of concealed piping and duct changes made during construction. The architect's agreement includes record drawings as a supplemental service. The contractor kept marked-up drawings at the site throughout construction.

How should the architect prepare the record drawings?

options.text: Survey the concealed work and certify its locations
options.explanation: The architect can't verify concealed conditions and shouldn't certify them.

options.text: Base them on the contractor's marked-up drawings
options.explanation: Correct. Record drawings compile the changes the contractor reported in its as-built markups.

options.text: Reissue the construction documents unchanged
options.explanation: That doesn't show the changes made during construction.

options.text: Base them on the approved shop drawings
options.explanation: Shop drawings show proposed work, not necessarily what was installed.

questions.explanation: Record drawings are based on the contractor's as-built markups and aren't verified by the architect.
questions.confidenceNote: Per A201-2017 §3.11 and B101 supplemental services list.

questions.stem:
During construction of a corporate office, the architect will issue several revision bulletins with revised drawing sheets. On the firm's last project, the contractor priced a change from an outdated sheet, and the owner and contractor argued about which version was current.

Which practices would help avoid a repeat of that problem? Check the three that apply.

options.text: Revision clouds and deltas on revised sheets
options.explanation: Correct. They show exactly what changed.

options.text: Updated issue dates in each title block's log
options.explanation: Correct. The issue log shows which version is current.

options.text: Transmittals listing the revised sheets
options.explanation: Correct. They record what was issued, to whom and when.

options.text: Replacing sheets without marking the changes
options.explanation: Unmarked changes are easy to miss and hard to price.

options.text: Describing changes only in email text
options.explanation: Email alone doesn't revise the contract documents.

options.text: Reissuing the full set for every minor change
options.explanation: Full reissues hide the few sheets that changed.

questions.explanation: Revisions: clouds and deltas, title-block log, transmittals.

questions.stem:
For a new museum, the architect wants the contractor's engineer to design the feature stair's steel stringers and connections. The architect will define the stair's geometry and finishes. The specifications must make clear what the contractor's engineer is responsible for and what the architect will review.

What should the architect's documents provide for the stair?

options.text: Complete structural calculations for the stair
options.explanation: Providing full calculations defeats the purpose of delegating the design.

options.text: Performance and design criteria for the stair
options.explanation: Correct. The documents state the criteria. The contractor's licensed engineer designs and seals the work, and the architect reviews it for conformance with the design concept.

options.text: A note that the contractor is responsible for the stair
options.explanation: A note without criteria leaves the requirements undefined.

options.text: A manufacturer's catalog number for a stock stair
options.explanation: A stock product doesn't meet a custom feature-stair design.

questions.explanation: Delegated design: state performance and design criteria. The contractor's professional seals the design.

questions.stem:
An owner, architect and contractor have signed an integrated project delivery agreement for a medical center. The team will share building information models, and the owner wants to know what the models will contain at each milestone, so the contractor can rely on them for estimating at the right times.

What should define model content at each milestone?

options.text: Level-of-development definitions in the BIM plan
options.explanation: Correct. LOD definitions set what each model element must contain, and how reliable it is, at each milestone.

options.text: The architect's standard CAD layer conventions
options.explanation: Layer standards organize files but don't define content or reliability.

options.text: The software vendor's default model templates
options.explanation: Vendor templates don't reflect the team's agreed deliverables.

options.text: The contractor's estimating software requirements
options.explanation: The contractor's needs are one input. The agreed plan governs.

questions.explanation: IPD/BIM: levels of development in the BIM execution plan define model content by milestone.
questions.confidenceNote: AIA E203/G202 BIM documents; confirm editions.

flashcards.back: Complete CDs and project manual, priceable as a fixed sum. Allowances and alternates for open decisions.
GMP set (often DD), reconciled assumptions and clarifications, early-release packages.
Program, concept and performance criteria (often about 30% design). Detailed design is left to the design-builder.
States the required results and criteria. Used in design-build and delegated design.
Written scope for each package, graphic limits, responsibility list for interface items.
A set amount in the bid for an owner decision that isn't final. The contract sum is adjusted later.
The bid set with addenda incorporated, for construction (B101 supplemental service).
